newsitem.title: QATAR: Interpol says Gulf vital transit point for drugs.
newsitem.headline: Interpol says Gulf vital transit point for drugs.

text.p: The Gulf has become a vital transit point for illegal drugs, channelling narcotics such as heroin, opium, and cocaine to users across the globe, Interpol officials said on Saturday.

"The Gulf area is less affected by the drug problem than other world regions...But it has become an essential transit point for various drugs manufactured in other parts of the world," Interpol Secretary-General Raymond Kendall said.

Speaking at the "Milipol 96" international conference on the fight against drugs, Kendall said over 50 percent of Interpol's current activities concentrated on detecting drugs routes and stopping the trade.
Anti-drug officials from 18 countries are participating in the three-day conference, which opened in Doha on Saturday under the auspices of Interpol and Qatar's ministry of interior.
In a bid to stem the billion-dollar drugs trade, participants called for a crackdown on producers, middlemen and distributors of narcotics, primarily heroin, cocaine, cannabis and synthetic drugs.
"The drug traffic involves the nexus of three parties -- chemical producers, intermediary traders and distributors," said Gene Haislip of the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration.
"If we set up a small cell of drug specialists in customs, police and trade offices in different countries, I am sure we can reduce the magnitude of the problem," he said.
R. Sundaralingam, a drugs consultant at Interpol, said the Gulf region was becoming a trade hub for various drugs including the opiate heroin.
"Every airport in Asia and the Gulf is an embarkation point and every country in Europe and the south and north America is destination for heroin", he said.
Sundaralingam singled out Afghanistan as a key heroin supplier.

"Because of political turmoil and civil strife, agriculture has been totally destroyed and the drug industry has flourished in Afghanistan, supplying more than 1,000 tonnes of opium to the world," he said.
Studies showed Afghanistan has over 100 illicit laboratories producing 100 tonnes of heroin a year. A kilogramme of heroin fetches $50,000 in Europe.
Sundaralingam said the Gulf region was also becoming a "half-way house" for cannabis, because many local people abused the drug, making the area an ideal route for the billion-dollar illicit trade.
